title: Deadline day
goal: Describe players with relative clauses, negotiate a transfer and defend a decision.
warmup: Which player would you buy for your favourite club? Why?
Describe a player in one sentence with who or whose.
Is it better to buy a young player or an experienced one?

main.task: Choose two of the three players; negotiate with the agent; announce the signing at a press conference.
main.howto: Use who, which, where, whose every time you describe a player. Negotiation: That's too much. · Our final offer is… · Take it or leave it.
prompts: The decision: which two players and why?
The negotiation: £15 million vs £20 million
The press conference: why did you choose him?

followup: Describe a player from your own team like a scout.
Should clubs spend so much money on players?
teacher: Catch 'which' for people and 'who's' for 'whose'. Disagree as the owner to make him defend his choice. Keep the agent tough!

title: The name game
goal: Talk about names, nicknames and their history using the passive: be called, be known as, be named after, was founded by.
warmup: Have you got a nickname? Where does it come from?
Which English club do you like most? What's its nickname?
What is your town famous for?

main.task: Guess the club from passive clues; talk about nicknames of Ukrainian clubs; invent your own club — name, kit, badge and fans' nickname.
main.howto: Use the passive whenever you can: It's called… It was named after… It was founded by… They're known as…
prompts: Guess the club from three clues
Nicknames of Ukrainian clubs — real or invented
Your own club: name, colours, badge, fans

phrases: On the badge you can see…
followup: Should clubs keep old names or change them?
Which nickname from the text do you like most? Why?
teacher: Catch missing 'be' (The club founded…) and V1 instead of V3 on the spot. Push for the passive in every answer about history.

title: What's he like?
goal: Describe people's personality with adjectives, examples and correct articles.
warmup: Which three words describe you?
What's your best friend like?
Who do you take after?

main.task: Describe four people: your best friend, your coach or a teacher, someone you take after, yourself. Then play Guess who with famous footballers.
main.howto: Three personality words for each person, and an example for each word. Use a / an / the: He's a really patient man. He's the most reliable player in the team.
prompts: your best friend
your coach or a teacher
someone in your family
yourself — one good and one not-so-good quality
a famous footballer (Guess who)

phrases: He's the most … person I know.
followup: Who would you choose as captain — Danylo, Artem or Bohdan? Why?
Is it better to be talented or hard-working?
teacher: Insist on an example after every adjective. Catch 'I'm student', 'play the football', 'a honest' on the spot.

title: Press conference
goal: Ask questions in different tenses as a journalist, and give full answers with interview phrases as a player.
warmup: How do you feel today?
What are you looking forward to this week?
Who do you look up to?

main.task: Pick a scenario: the hero, the bad day, the big move, the comeback. One of us is the player, the other the journalist — then swap.
main.howto: Journalist: six questions in six different forms. Player: full answers, three interview phrases, three verbs from Lesson 8.
prompts: You scored the winner in the cup final.
You lost 4–0 and missed a penalty.
At 17 you've just signed for a big European club.
Your first match after a long injury.

phrases: What was going through your mind?
I have to give credit to…
We take it one game at a time.
followup: Interview me for the school newspaper — then tell me three facts about me.
Hot seat: 60 seconds of fast questions.
teacher: Score a point for every question in a new tense and every question that ends with a preposition. Catch 'Where you were…' and 'Who did score' on the spot. Push for a detail in every answer.

title: Questions with a partner
goal: Answer and ask questions with phrasal verbs and verbs with prepositions, using the same verb in the answer plus one detail.
warmup: Who do you take after?
When did you take up football?
Who do you look up to?

main.task: I ask, you answer — then you ask me the same question.
main.howto: Answer with the same verb and add one detail in the Past Simple.
prompts: What are you looking forward to this month?
Who do you get on best with in your team?
Have you ever taken part in a competition?
What does a good match depend on?
What do people your age complain about most?
What would you like to take up next?

phrases: I took up … when I was…
I really look up to … because…
followup: Have you ever had to get over a bad defeat?
Who do you rely on most?
teacher: Insist on the same verb in the answer. Catch 'looking forward to see' and 'depend from' on the spot.

title: The GOAT debate
goal: Argue about the greatest player or team with facts, using as … as (just / nearly / not nearly / twice), whereas / although and superlatives with ever.
warmup: Who is your favourite player? What position does he play?
Which team do you support, and why?
What's the best match you've ever watched?

main.task: Pick a pair and argue for your side for one minute. Then I take the other side and you argue back.
main.howto: Use at least two as … as (one with just / nearly / not nearly), one whereas or although, and one superlative with ever.
prompts: Messi or Ronaldo?
Pelé or Maradona?
Real Madrid or Barcelona?
Dynamo or Shakhtar?
Premier League or La Liga?
playing football or watching it?

phrases: He's the most … player I've ever seen.
followup: Who is the best player in your class? Compare yourself with him.
Is it fair to compare players from different generations?
teacher: Push for numbers and facts, not just 'he is better'. Catch 'as … than', 'two times bigger' and 'plays as good as' on the spot. When he's comfortable, take the opposite side even if you agree with him.

title: Which is better?
goal: Compare two things with reasons, and use superlatives with the Present Perfect: the best … I've ever …
warmup: Which is better: summer or winter? Give two reasons.
Who is the funniest person you know?
What's the best film you've ever seen?

main.task: Choose one pair and argue for your side for one minute. Then I take the other side.
main.howto: Say which one you prefer and why. Use at least three comparatives and one 'not as … as'. Finish with a superlative: 'It's the best … I've ever …'
prompts: city or village?
phone or laptop?
skateboard or bike?
school trip or holiday with family?
pizza or burger?
online lessons or lessons at school?

phrases: I think … is much better than …
followup: What's the most dangerous thing you've ever done?
What's the most expensive thing you've ever bought?
teacher: Force the 'because' after every comparison. Catch 'more better' and 'than/then' on the spot. The follow-ups mix today's topic with Lesson 5 — insist on Past Simple for the details.

title: Have you ever…?
goal: Ask about experiences in the Present Perfect and keep the conversation going with Past Simple follow-up questions.
warmup: Name three things you've done this week that you didn't do last week.
What's the most unusual food you've ever tried?
Name one place you've never been to but really want to see.

main.task: Interview: find three experiences we both have and three that only one of us has.
main.howto: Ask a 'Have you ever…?' question. If the answer is Yes, ask at least two follow-up questions in the Past Simple. Then answer my questions the same way — never just 'Yes, I have.'
prompts: Have you ever got lost somewhere?
Have you ever broken a bone?
Have you ever met someone famous?
Have you ever stayed up all night?
Have you ever won something?
Have you ever been really embarrassed in public?
Have you ever slept in a tent?
Have you ever tried a sport that went badly?

phrases: No, I haven't, but I'd love to…
I've done it a couple of times.
How did you feel? — I was absolutely…
followup: Which experience from your list would you like to repeat?
What's the next thing you want to try? Why?
teacher: Hold him to two follow-ups after every 'Yes'. Switch tense out loud if he stays in the Present Perfect for the details: 'When? → Past Simple.' Push the strong adjectives from Lesson 4 in the 'How did you feel?' answers.

title: The day it all went wrong
goal: Tell a story in the past: keep the background in the Past Continuous and the events in the Past Simple.
warmup: What is the worst weather you have ever walked home in?
When did you last oversleep? What happened next?
Tell me about a small thing that ruined a whole day.

main.task: Tell the story of a day that went wrong — yours, or invented.
main.howto: Two minutes. Set the scene first (what was going on), then the events one after another. Use at least three linkers and two strong adjectives.
prompts: How did the day start? What were you doing when it went wrong?
What happened first — and then?
How did you feel at that moment? Use a strong adjective, not 'very'.
Was there a moment when it got even worse?
How did it end? Were you relieved, or was it still awful?

phrases: By the time I got there…
I was absolutely freezing / starving / exhausted.
And then, to make things worse…
followup: Is it funny now, or still annoying?
Whose fault was it, honestly?
What would you do differently if the same morning happened tomorrow?
teacher: Let him finish the whole story without corrections, then replay two or three sentences back with the tense fixed — he hears the difference better than he reads it.

title: A day in your life
goal: Talk about your routine in the Present Simple and switch to the Present Continuous when you describe today.
warmup: What time did you wake up today? Was that early or late for you?
What is the first thing you do after you get up?
Are you a morning person or a night person? Why?

main.task: Describe your normal Wednesday, then say how today is different.
main.howto: Speak for about two minutes without stopping. Use at least four time expressions and switch to the Present Continuous when you talk about today.
prompts: Morning: what time, in what order, how long it takes you
School: when it starts, when you have a break, when you get home
Afternoon: homework, hobbies, friends
Evening: dinner, screens, what time you go to bed
And today? What is different from a normal Wednesday?

phrases: It takes me about twenty minutes to…
On weekdays I… , at the weekend I…
followup: If you could change one thing about your morning, what would it be?
Whose routine in your family is the strangest?
Would you like to start school at 10 a.m.? What would you lose?
teacher: Count out loud how many times the tense switch is correct and say the number at the end — it turns accuracy into a small game.

title: Free time and hobbies
goal: Talk about hobbies with play / go / do and tell a short story about the past.
warmup: What did you do last weekend?
How often do you do your hobby — every day, twice a week, or less?
Which hobby would you never try? Why not?

main.task: Tell the story of how you started your hobby.
main.howto: Two minutes, in the past. Begin with when it started and finish with how it is going now.
prompts: When and how did you start? Who showed you?
What was difficult at the beginning?
Tell one funny or bad moment — what happened?
How often do you do it now?
Would you like to be really good at it, or is it just for fun?

phrases: I took it up when I was…
At first it was hard because…
One day I was… when suddenly…
I'm quite good at… / I'm not very good at…
followup: Is it better to have one hobby or many?
Do your parents think your hobby is useful?
What hobby do you think you will have at 30?
teacher: If the story dries up after three sentences, ask 'and then what happened?' twice — it usually doubles the length.

title: Getting to know you
goal: Give longer answers about yourself instead of one word.
warmup: Tell me three things about yourself — one of them false. I'll guess which.
Describe your best friend in five sentences.
What are you good at that people don't expect?

main.task: Describe a person in your family without saying who it is.
main.howto: Speak for a minute and a half. I have to guess the person from your description.
prompts: What do they look like?
What do they do every day?
What makes them different from everyone else?
What do you argue about?
What have you learnt from them?

phrases: The thing about him / her is…
What I like about them is…
followup: Who in your family are you most like?
Is it easier to describe someone you love or someone you don't?
teacher: Ban one-word answers out loud at the start — 'every answer is at least two sentences' — and hold to it.
